               OKLAHOMA SUSTAINABILITY NETWORK’S STATEMENT OF POSITION

                 Oklahoma Sustainability Network (OSN), by and through its undersigned counsel,

         respectfully submits the following Statement of Position in the above-captioned Cause. OSN is a

         501(c)(3) nonprofit, founded in 1999, that strives to connect and educate the people of Oklahoma

         concerning the many aspects of sustainability, and to contribute practical ideas linking a prosperous

         economy with a healthy environment and thriving communities. OSN supports cost-effective

         policies and projects that encourage market innovation, economic security, environmental

         responsibility, and societal benefits. OSN’s board of directors includes members with expertise

         ranging from environmental economics, medical science, and public policy to public relations,

         transportation, and air quality policies and issues.1

                 OSN has carefully reviewed the application, testimony, and discovery responses provided

         by Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company (“OG&E”) in this Cause. At a structural level, the

         proposed Extra Large Power and Light (“XLPL”) Tariff and its Terms and Conditions of Service

         for Extra Large Load Customers (“T&CXLLC”) responds appropriately to Oklahoma House Bill

         2992 and the Commission’s Order No. 753440: Contribution in aid of construction (“CIAC”)



         1
            OSN is a 501(c)(3) registered non-profit, non-partisan organization. More information is available at
         https://www.oksustainability.org.

                                                            1
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 47 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/22/2026 - PAGE 2 OF 34




        funding, the minimum term, termination and capacity reduction fees, collateral, minimum billing

        levels, and the Customer Class Protection Charge all compare favorable to other large load tariffs

        considered across the U.S.

                   But OSN is concerned that OG&E’s responses to important data requests follow a clear

        pattern: wherever a specific timeline, methodology, or number is required to implement the tariff

        as described, OG&E defers it, either to an as-yet defined proceeding, a different docket, or a

        determination following a specific dispute.

                   This risk is compounded by OG&E’s statement that it will not file individual Electric

        Service Agreements (ESAs) with the Commission for approval at all. Rather, they will seek only

        approval of the standard form agreement filed here.2 Most of the determinations discussed below,

        including cost allocation and customer protection, will therefore be determined within agreements

        that might never reach the Commission for review.

                   OSN’s recommendations identify specific steps the Commission can take to ensure the

        stated goals of establishing this tariff, and of House Bill 2992, are met. These recommendations

        aim to avoid a future where new ESAs and related issues are litigated piecemeal, years down the

        road, in forums where the Commission and Oklahoma ratepayers might have no access.


        Recommendations:

              1. The Commission should require OG&E to itemize, in each approved agreement, which

                   cost categories are recovered through CIAC and which are not, as well as how those

                   additional costs are allocated.




        2
            OIEC 01-09, Sep. 9, 2026.

                                                         2
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 47 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/22/2026 - PAGE 3 OF 34




            2. The Commission should adopt and require OG&E’s commitment to a with-and-without

               analysis of the Customer Class Protection Charge and set a no-later-than date for the first

               assessment.

            3. The Commission should approve both the minimum energy charge and minimum demand

               charge as written.

            4. The Commission should require OG&E to (1) make clear when and by what methodology

               the Customer Affordability Charge will be determined and whether it will include specific

               incremental additional benefits, (2) demonstrate that the CAC benefits customers on a

               specific need basis, rather than seniors as an undifferentiated group, or whether it will

               simply be used as a generic bill credit, and (3) identify the actual line-item costs the

               Reservation Charge is intended to recover and how the revenue would be applied to

               residential bills. As an alternative to the CAC, OSN recommends consideration of Google's

               proposal for an affordability and efficiency rider for large-load customers, with funding

               dedicated to low-to-moderate income residential customers.

            5. The Commission should require OG&E to demonstrate, specifically, why participation in

               any of the excluded riders would increase risk to customers or the utility. Otherwise, the

               Commission should direct OG&E to remove the blanket exclusion.

            6. The Commission should require OG&E to make some curtailable or flexible service option

               available, whether by lifting the Load Reduction Rider exclusion or developing a specific

               substitute for the XLPL Tariff.

            7. The Commission should decline to treat OG&E’s blanket legal objection as a substitute for

               a substantive, case-specific evaluation of whether a BYOG or similar self-supply

               arrangement would be appropriate for any customer covered under the XLPL tariff.



                                                        3
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 47 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/22/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 34




            8. The Commission should require that OG&E allow the same capacity purchase agreement

                (CPA) model approved in Case No. PUD2026-000031.



        Discussion:

            1. The XLPL tariff includes elements that provide reasonable protection against

                stranded cost risk. However, OG&E’s responses about covered investments raise

                major concerns about cost tracking and allocation.

            OSN agrees with Witness DeCourcey’s characterization of the XLPL tariff elements as being

        at least as protective as tariffs instituted by other utilities, and more protective than most.3 The

        elements included (a fifteen-year term, CIAC requirement, and financial assurance provisions) are

        sound, and OSN supports their approval.

                These elements are only as complete as the definition of covered investments. When asked

        to identify investment categories serving XLPL customer that would not be recovered through

        CIAC, OG&E responded that it “cannot reliability estimate all categories of investment that may

        be required … and that would not be recovered through” CIAC.4 When asked about ongoing

        operational costs and property taxes for infrastructure serving XLPL customers, OG&E responded

        that it “does not track costs… by individual asset or line” and that XLPL customers “will pay their

        appropriate allocated share… through the allocation process in the cost of service study.” That cost

        allocation process has not yet been designed or initiated, even with new eligible customers to come

        online in the near future.5




        3
          Direct Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey, pp. 15-18.
        4
          AARP 01-01, Aug. 21, 2026.
        5
          AG 01-05, Aug. 21, 2026.

                                                              4
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 47 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/22/2026 - PAGE 5 OF 34




                OG&E also stated that it performed no XLPL-specific cost-of-service analysis before

        proposing rates, and simply carried over LPL-TOU rates,6 and further stated that transmission or

        distribution upgrades will be “studied at the time that the cost is incurred,” with no formula or

        allocation method identified in advance.7

                If operational and other costs not covered by a narrow definition in CIAC are simply

        allocated across the entire customer base rather than to the XLPL class, the premise that large

        customers will “pay 100% of the costs to connect to the grid”8 is only speculative, and unable to

        be validated until well into a future rate case, after investments have been made.

                The Commission should require OG&E to itemize, in each approved agreement, which

        cost categories are recovered through CIAC and which are not, as well as how those additional

        costs are allocated.



            2. The Customer Class Protection Charge is a sound “fail-safe” mechanism

                conceptually, but it lacks a specific trigger and, by OG&E’s definition, is non-

                retroactive.

                The Customer Class Protection Charge is, as a concept, sensible: initially $0.00/kW-month,

        it gives the Commission a recurring opportunity to determine whether the XLPL class causes

        adverse rate impacts and, if so, set the charge to remedy them.9 OSN supports this conceptual

        structure.

                Unfortunately, neither the Tariff nor the Terms & Conditions define “adverse impact,” the

        methodology for measuring it, or the schedule for first assessing it – only that it will be reviewed



        6
          Google 03-02, Sep. 1, 2026.
        7
          Google 03-04, Sep. 1, 2026.
        8
          Direct Testimony of Gwin Cash, p 14-15.
        9
          Direct Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop, p. 10-11.

                                                           5
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 47 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/22/2026 - PAGE 6 OF 34




        at each general rate case and Fuel Adjustment Clause review.10 In fact, when responding to three

        potential methodologies in data requests, and when asked to state a specific interval, timeline and

        methodology, OG&E deferred to rebuttal testimony in a different proceeding and failed to take

        any position.11 There will be no cost-of-service study until the general rate case following the first

        XLPL customer’s service, and there is no estimate of when that will be. 12 A fail-safe that cannot

        be triggered until an indeterminate date is not, in practice, a fail-safe.

                OG&E, to its credit, committed to performing “a with and without study to determine any

        adverse impacts to other classes related to the addition of XLPL customers” in each general rate

        case.13 Notably, in the same response, OG&E states that the mechanism isn’t retroactive, given

        that general rate cases are solely forward looking.14

                To remedy these inconsistencies, the Commission should adopt and require OG&E’s

        commitment to a with-and-without analysis and set a no-later-than date for the first assessment.



             3. The paired minimum billing floors are a genuinely, unusually durable protection, and

                OSN supports their approval.

                The proposed tariff pairs an 85 percent minimum demand charge with a 90 percent

        minimum energy charge,15 covering both capacity and energy risk better than most tariffs, which

        rely solely on demand-based minimums. OSN supports this approach as it reduces risk for

        ratepayers and recommends that the Commission approve both charges as written.




        10
           Cash Direct, p.15-16.
        11
           AARP, 01-03, 01-04, Aug. 21, 2026.
        12
           AARP 01-7, Aug. 21, 2026.
        13
           PUD 07-02, a-b, Aug. 13, 2026.
        14
           PUD 07-02, d, Aug. 13, 2026.
        15
           Cash Direct, p.8-10.

                                                           6
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 47 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/22/2026 - PAGE 7 OF 34




                   The minimum energy charge serves a distinct purpose: OG&E must plan for each

        customer’s hourly energy use, not just its peak, and without the minimum, the utility risks

        preparing for that use whether or not it materializes. The floor still allows price responsiveness. A

        large customer remains free to adjust its consumption above the floor; the minimum simply ensures

        that OG&E recovers the costs of energy procured on the customer’s behalf. Voluntary curtailment

        or demand response can – and should - still be encouraged through a defined program or rider.



               4. As currently designed, the Customer Affordability Charge might not benefit the

                   customers OG&E claims it will. Indeed, OG&E’s own work shows that the benefit is

                   smaller and less targeted than they claim.

                   OSN supports the Customer Affordability Charge (“CAC”) as a legitimate mechanism in

        concept and does not dispute the claim that the charge as modeled may raise “more than $400

        million” for distribution to customers.16 However, it is critical that the collected dollars be

        distributed to those customers who need them most, and that is still in question.

                   Unfortunately, the underlying rate is less targeted than OG&E represented. Witness Shoop

        testified that the rate was designed to collect $30 million annually, reflecting the cost of the Low-

        Income Assistance Program (LIAP), “an expanded Senior Discount for all residential customers

        who qualify as senior citizens,” and 20 percent of the residential energy efficiency program.17

        Witness Shoop’s description implies that there will be some type of direct funding or even

        additional funding (e.g., expanded Senior Discount) for these valuable, recognized programs.

                   OG&E’s own work papers show the actual total to be $25,503,164 (about 15% less than

        represented), of which the expanded Senior Citizen Discount comprises over 50 percent


        16
             AG 03-03, Aug. 25, 2026.
        17
             Shoop Direct, p.11.

                                                          7
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 47 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/22/2026 - PAGE 8 OF 34




        ($12,897,390) which, unlike LIAP or certain energy efficiency programs, extends to all seniors

        regardless of means.18 Critically, eligibility for the program hinges on age rather than need, but

        OG&E has not actually decided how the funds will be deployed, deferring again to an undefined

        Commission determination.19 This same vagueness exists for the Reservation Charge – OG&E

        confirmed that which customers, the interval at which the charge is assessed, and how it will appear

        on a bill, will be “determined in a future proceeding” by the Commission.20

                Further, and as OSN raised in PUD Case No. 2026-000031, OG&E has not addressed why

        the charge’s benefit is limited to residential customers when small commercial customers may face

        comparable affordability pressure from new large load.

                The Commission should require OG&E to (1) make clear when and by what methodology

        the CAC will be determined and which specific incremental additional benefits it will contribute

        to, (2) demonstrate that the CAC benefits customers on a specific need basis, rather than seniors

        as an undifferentiated group, and (3) identify the actual cost the Reservation Charge is intended to

        recover.

                As an alternative to the CAC, OSN finds significant merit in Google's proposal to establish

        a volumetric charge that would provide funding for residential energy efficiency upgrades,

        described by Google as an affordability and efficiency rider for large-load customers, with funds

        distributed by an appropriate State of Oklahoma office.21 Notably, recent EIA data shows

        Oklahoma has the nation's highest residential customer electricity disconnection rate.22 OSN has

        a long history of supporting cost-effective energy efficiency programs in Oklahoma and offers its

        full assistance with development of this mechanism.



             5. The blanket exclusion of XLPL customers from voluntary clean energy programs is

                not justified in this or other related proceedings.

                The XLPL tariff, as proposed, bars customers from the Green Power Wind Rider,

        Renewable Energy Program, Utility Solar Program, Load Reduction Rider, Day-Ahead Pricing

        and Flex Price schedules, the Economic Development Incentive Credit Rider, and the Energizing

        Renewable Connections Rider.23 Unlike the other provisions included in the tariff, no OG&E

        witness explains why participation in any of these riders would increase risk to either customers

        or the utility. These are voluntary, opt-in programs funded by the participating customer’s own

        incremental cost.

                When initially asked about the blanket disallowance, and asked to justify each exclusion

        individually, OG&E gave the same brief answer of all: it “deemed it most prudent to protect

        existing customers’ use of these optional programs,” but provided no measure of prudency or

        analysis to justify this claim.24 In response to a subsequent data request, OG&E still did not provide

        a measure of prudency, but they stated that individual requests for Renewable Energy or RECs

        would be addressed on a case-by-case basis..25 This response provides no assurance that these

        important tariff options will be available for new customers, and it does not explain why the

        established, proven programs could not be utilized.




        23
           Cash Direct, p.6.
        24
           OSN 02-02, Sep. 3, 2026.
        25
           OSN 03-02(b)(ii), Sep. 21, 2026 (stating, for example, that “OG&E will manage individual requests for RECs on a
        case-by-case basis, rather than through the Renewable Energy Program”).

                                                                9
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 47 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/22/2026 - PAGE 10 OF 34




                OSN also flagged this issue as unresolved in the OG&E-Google ESA docket, PUD 2026-

        000031; it should be resolved here. The Commission should require OG&E to demonstrate,

        specifically, why participation in any of these riders would increase risk to customers or the utility.

        Otherwise, the Commission should direct OG&E to remove the blanket exclusion.



             6. A demand response or flexibility option should be required. The tariff does not merely

                omit a requirement; it bars any voluntary participation in such programs.

                OG&E confirmed that the XLPL Tariff “does not allow subscription to the Company’s

        Load Reduction Rider,” when referring to the Applicability section of the tariff, and justifies the

        approach by stating that no XLPL applicant has expressed willingness to limit withdrawals.26

        OG&E stated that it is “evaluating options for XLPL” but that a proposal will not be ready until a

        pending FERC proceeding resolves SPP’s load modifier rules, again with no estimated date.27

                Cost-effective flexibility mechanisms provide great promise, particularly in systems across

        the country facing impending load growth. Yet those mechanisms are excluded in this proposal.

        Existing customers should not be forced to accept that the lowest cost, lowest risk capacity resource

        - load flexibility - will be ignored in favor of higher cost supply-side resources.

                Indeed, OG&E already successfully operates load flexibility programs. Their Business

        Demand Response program, which includes data centers, saved over 21 MW in 2025, at a cost of

        just $128/kW.28 Even this modest amount of load reduction can prove crucial during critical hours

        when the grid is under maximum stress and SPP market prices are high. At a larger scale, OG&E's

        current Load Reduction program is forecast to reduce demand by more than 900 MW in 2027 for




        26
           PUD 09-04, Aug. 18, 2026
        27
           OIEC 01-08, a, Sep. 11, 2026
        28
           OG&E Oklahoma Comprehensive Demand Program Portfolio, 2025 Annual Report, July 2026, pp 5 & 7.

                                                           10
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 47 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/22/2026 - PAGE 11 OF 34




         the summer season, and by more than 1000 MW during the winter peak. OSN notes that OG&E’s

         2026 IRP treats Load Reduction Programs as a specific capacity resource.29

                 An active, established, load management program for major data centers could encourage

         these large customers to include load flexibility in the design of their facilities, rather than

         attempting to add that flexibility at a later date, when practical challenges might limit potential.

                 The Commission should require OG&E to make some curtailable or flexible service option

         available, whether by lifting the Load Reduction Rider exclusion or developing a specific

         substitute for the XLPL Tariff.



              7. OG&E’s blanket objection to bring-your-own-generation (BYOG) arrangements

                 should not substitute for a case-specific evaluation.

                 In response to a PUD data request, OG&E stated that, in this case, they “did not include a

         BYOG option”, referring to the positions taken in OG&E’s public comment filed in Case No.

         PUD2025-000075.30 As OSN previously raised, in its Statement of Position filed in Case No.

         PUD2026-000031, properly structured BYOG arrangements, already present in other jurisdictions,

         can reduce a utility’s incremental generation and capacity obligations associated with serving

         large, new loads, and should not be foreclosed as a category. Grand River Dam Authority, for

         example, allows large customers to source renewable and supplemental supply through its

         Schedule LGS-SS (Large General Service – Supplemental Supply) and associated Renewable

         Rider, rather than treating self-supply as categorically off-limits.31 Evergy Kansas employs a

         Customer Capacity Rider, which allows the utility to credit large customers for supplying SPP-

 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 47 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/22/2026 - PAGE 12 OF 34




         accredited generation capacity32, and the Georgia Public Service Commission approved a

         Customer Identified Resource program allowing large customers to directly negotiate with project

         developers and partner to submit a bid to the utility’s Clean and Renewable Energy subscription

         program.33

                 OG&E’s response both in this and in the Google contract case relies entirely on a legal

         position taken in a separate proceeding and makes clear that BYOG has not been considered as a

         feasible alternative. OSN recommends the Commission decline to treat OG&E’s blanket legal

         objection as a substitute for a substantive, case-specific evaluation of whether a BYOG or similar

         self-supply arrangement would be appropriate for any customer covered under the XLPL tariff.

                 Further, the Commission should require that OG&E allow the same capacity purchase

         agreement (CPA) model approved in the Google case (PUD2026-000031), for consideration in

         future customer agreements, as they demonstrate an opportunity to bring new capacity onto

         Oklahoma utility systems without exposing all customers to construction, financing, or

         performance risk.



         Recommendations:

         Please find OSN’s recommendations, discussed above and restated here:

              1. The Commission should require OG&E to itemize, in each approved agreement, which

                 cost categories are recovered through CIAC and which are not, as well as how those

                 additional costs are allocated.

            2. The Commission should adopt and require OG&E’s commitment to a with-and-without

               analysis of the Customer Class Protection Charge and set a no-later-than date for the first

               assessment.

            3. The Commission should approve both the minimum energy charge and minimum demand

               the Customer Affordability Charge will be determined and whether it will include specific

               incremental additional benefits, (2) demonstrate that the CAC benefits customers on a

               specific need basis, rather than seniors as an undifferentiated group, or whether it will

               simply be used as a generic bill credit, and (3) identify the actual line-item costs the

            6. The Commission should require OG&E to make some curtailable or flexible service option

            7. The Commission should decline to treat OG&E’s blanket legal objection as a substitute for

               a substantive, case-specific evaluation of whether a BYOG or similar self-supply

               arrangement would be appropriate for any custom covered under the XLPL tariff.

            8. The Commission should require that OG&E allow the same capacity purchase agreement

        or to amend and/or supplement this Statement of Position as necessary if new material evidence

        becomes available. Further, OSN's position is limited to the issues discussed herein and any issue

        omitted does not indicate that OSN agrees or disagrees with other Parties’ assertions.
